title: Testing & Debugging asyncio: The Handwritten Field Guide
summary: How to test async Python with pytest-asyncio, IsolatedAsyncioTestCase and AsyncMock, and how to debug event-loop problems with debug mode, slow-callback logs, never-awaited warnings, tracemalloc, task inspection and deterministic timeout tests.

chapters.title: Why Async Code Needs Special Testing
points: Calling an async def function only creates a coroutine object. Nothing runs until an event loop drives it, so a plain test function that calls it checks nothing.

Plain pytest does not run async def tests. It skips them with a PytestUnhandledCoroutineWarning ('async def functions are not natively supported'), and older versions reported them as passing even though they never ran.
A test runner for async code has three jobs: create a loop, run the test coroutine until it finishes, then cancel leftover tasks and close the loop.
Behind every runner is asyncio.run(main()) or asyncio.Runner (3.11+). Each creates a fresh loop, runs the coroutine, shuts down async generators and the default executor, then closes the loop.
Awaiting interleaves tasks, so order bugs, races and missed awaits only show up under particular schedules. Tests should control scheduling instead of trusting timing.
Main bug types: a missing await, a task that is never awaited and gets lost, a blocking call that stalls the loop, a timeout that never fires, and an object used from a different loop.
Main tools: pytest-asyncio or IsolatedAsyncioTestCase run tests, AsyncMock replaces dependencies, debug mode and tracemalloc diagnose problems, and all_tasks/print_stack inspect what is running.
Mistake: calling asyncio.run() inside a test that is already running on a loop raises 'asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop'.
Mistake: creating asyncio primitives (Lock, Queue, Future) at import time. They can end up bound to a different loop than the one the test uses.

chapters.title: pytest-asyncio: Markers and Modes
points: Install pytest-asyncio and mark tests with @pytest.mark.asyncio on an async def test. The plugin runs the coroutine to completion on an event loop.
Strict mode is the default (asyncio_mode = strict). Only marked tests are handled, and async fixtures must use @pytest_asyncio.fixture. This lets it coexist with trio or anyio plugins.
Auto mode (asyncio_mode = auto in pytest.ini or pyproject) treats every async def test and fixture as asyncio, so no markers are needed. Use it only when asyncio is your sole async library.
Apply the marker to a whole module with pytestmark = pytest.mark.asyncio. On a class, decorate the class and every async method is covered.
Example: @pytest.mark.asyncio async def test_fetch(): assert await fetch(1) == {'id': 1}
Comparison: strict mode is explicit and safe with multiple async libraries. Auto mode has less boilerplate but claims every coroutine test.
Mixing sync and async tests in one file is fine. Sync tests never touch the loop.
Mistake: decorating an async fixture with a plain @pytest.fixture in strict mode. The test receives an un-awaited coroutine or async generator instead of the value.
Mistake: forgetting the marker in strict mode. The test is skipped with a warning and your CI stays green without running it.
Tip: pytest -W error turns the 'unhandled coroutine' warning into a failure, so an unmarked test can't slip through.

chapters.title: Event Loop Scope and Async Fixtures
points: loop_scope sets how long one event loop lives: function (the default, a new loop per test), class, module, package or session.
Tests: @pytest.mark.asyncio(loop_scope='module') runs every test in the module on one shared loop.

Fixtures: @pytest_asyncio.fixture(loop_scope='session', scope='session') puts an expensive resource, such as a DB pool, on a long-lived loop. loop_scope may not be narrower than the fixture's caching scope.
Set asyncio_default_fixture_loop_scope in config. pytest-asyncio 0.24+ warns while it is unset.
Async generator fixture: async def client(): c = await connect(); yield c; await c.close(). Code after the yield is async teardown, run on the same loop.
The old pattern of overriding the event_loop fixture to change scope was deprecated in 0.22+ and removed in 1.0. Use loop_scope instead.
Mistake: a session-scoped fixture used by function-loop tests raises 'Future attached to a different loop' or 'got Future attached to a different loop'. Align the loop_scope values.
Trade-off: a shared loop is faster (setup happens once) but state leaks between tests. A per-test loop isolates tests but pays for setup every time.
Leftover tasks from one test can keep running into the next when the loop is shared. Cancel and await them in fixture teardown.
Custom loops (for example uvloop): pytest-asyncio 1.x takes a loop policy or loop factory through an event_loop_policy fixture instead of a replaced event_loop.

chapters.title: unittest's IsolatedAsyncioTestCase
points: unittest.IsolatedAsyncioTestCase (3.8+) is the standard-library runner for async tests. Test methods can be async def and are awaited automatically.
Every test gets a brand-new event loop that is closed afterwards. That is where the 'Isolated' in the name comes from.
Lifecycle order: setUp, then asyncSetUp, then the test, then asyncTearDown, then tearDown, with cleanups last.
addAsyncCleanup(coro_fn, *args) registers an async cleanup that runs in LIFO order, even if the test fails.
The loop runs with debug=True, so slow callbacks and never-awaited coroutines are logged without extra setup.
When the test ends, the runner cancels still-pending tasks and awaits them, then shuts down async generators before closing the loop.
3.13+: set the class attribute loop_factory (for example uvloop.new_event_loop) to choose the loop implementation.
Example: class T(IsolatedAsyncioTestCase): async def asyncSetUp(self): self.db = await connect(); async def test_q(self): self.assertEqual(await self.db.get(1), 'a')
Comparison with pytest-asyncio: no extra dependency and a fixed per-test loop, but no fixture graph and no shared loop scope. pytest can still collect and run these classes.
Mistake: doing async work in setUpClass. It is synchronous and runs outside the loop, so shared async state has no class-level async hook.

chapters.title: Mocking Coroutines with AsyncMock
points: unittest.mock.AsyncMock (3.8+): calling it returns an awaitable, and awaiting that awaitable produces return_value.
side_effect options: an exception is raised when awaited; an iterable returns its next item on each await; an async function is awaited with the call's arguments.
Await-specific assertions: assert_awaited(), assert_awaited_once_with(...), assert_any_await, assert_has_awaits, plus the await_count and await_args attributes.
assert_called() versus assert_awaited(): a mock that was called but never awaited passes assert_called and fails assert_awaited, which is how you catch a missing await.
patch('mod.fetch') produces an AsyncMock automatically when the target is an async def. So does create_autospec on an async function.
MagicMock (3.8+) supports __aenter__/__aexit__ and __aiter__. Example: m.__aenter__.return_value = conn for 'async with pool.acquire() as conn'.
Mocking an async iterator: mock.__aiter__.return_value = [1, 2, 3], so 'async for' yields 1, 2, 3.
Example: fetch = AsyncMock(return_value={'id': 1}); assert await service(fetch) == 1; fetch.assert_awaited_once_with(1)
Mistake: using a plain Mock or MagicMock for a coroutine gives TypeError: object MagicMock can't be used in 'await' expression.
Mistake: return_value=asyncio.sleep(0) or another coroutine object. Awaiting the mock returns the coroutine itself, not its result, and the coroutine then leaks as never-awaited.

chapters.title: asyncio Debug Mode and Slow Callbacks
points: Four ways to turn debug mode on: asyncio.run(main(), debug=True), the environment variable PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1, python -X dev (Python Development Mode), or loop.set_debug(True).
Debug mode logs never-awaited coroutines together with the traceback of where they were created, using coroutine origin tracking.
Debug mode makes non-thread-safe calls such as loop.call_soon from another thread raise RuntimeError instead of silently corrupting the loop.
Slow callbacks: any callback or task step that takes longer than loop.slow_callback_duration (default 0.1 s) is logged as 'Executing <Task ...> took 0.253 seconds'.
Tune the threshold, for example loop.slow_callback_duration = 0.05, to catch smaller blocking calls such as time.sleep, sync I/O or heavy CPU work.
Debug mode also emits ResourceWarning for unclosed transports and event loops, and logs the source of the offending object.
Messages go to the 'asyncio' logger, so they only appear once logging is configured: logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG). Also enable warnings with -W default.
Fix for a slow callback: move blocking work to await asyncio.to_thread(fn) or loop.run_in_executor. Never block inside a coroutine.
Trade-off: debug mode adds noticeable overhead (tracebacks, extra checks). Keep it in tests and CI, not in production hot paths.

chapters.title: Never-Awaited Coroutines and tracemalloc
points: 'RuntimeWarning: coroutine 'fetch' was never awaited' is emitted when a coroutine object is garbage-collected without having run. It almost always means a missing await.
The warning fires at GC time, so it may appear far from the bug or be attributed to a different test.
The warning says 'Enable tracemalloc to get the object allocation traceback'. Run python -X tracemalloc=25 or set PYTHONTRACEMALLOC=25 to see where the coroutine was created.
tracemalloc records allocation stacks, and the number is the frame depth. It uses more memory and runs slower, so enable it only while debugging.
Debug mode sets sys.set_coroutine_origin_tracking_depth, which gives a similar creation traceback without tracemalloc.
'Task was destroyed but it is pending!' means a task was GC'd mid-flight. Keep a strong reference, for example tasks.add(t); t.add_done_callback(tasks.discard).
'Task exception was never retrieved' means a task failed and nobody awaited it or called .exception(), so the error was silently lost.
Make these warnings fail CI with pytest -W error::RuntimeWarning, or filterwarnings = error::RuntimeWarning in config.
Mistake: silencing the warning with a filter. The un-awaited call never ran, so the side effect it was supposed to have is missing.

chapters.title: Inspecting Live Tasks
points: asyncio.all_tasks() returns the set of not-yet-done tasks for the running loop. Call it from inside the loop, because without a running loop it raises RuntimeError.
asyncio.current_task() returns the task running the current coroutine, which is useful for logging and for excluding itself from all_tasks().
Name your tasks: asyncio.create_task(coro, name='poller') or t.set_name(). Names appear in reprs, logs and task dumps instead of 'Task-17'.
task.get_stack(limit=None) returns the frames where the task is suspended. task.print_stack(limit, file) prints them, which shows exactly which await it is stuck on.
task.get_coro() returns the wrapped coroutine. task.done(), cancelled() and exception() show its state.
Hang dump example: for t in asyncio.all_tasks(): if t is not asyncio.current_task(): t.print_stack()
Leak check in teardown: assert no tasks remain besides the current one after the test. Leftover tasks point to fire-and-forget bugs.
Python 3.14: python -m asyncio ps PID and python -m asyncio pstree PID inspect the task tree of a running process from outside.
Python 3.14: asyncio.print_call_graph() and capture_call_graph() show the chain of tasks awaiting one another, beyond a single task's stack.
Mistake: expecting all_tasks() to include finished tasks, or calling it from another thread. It only reports pending tasks of the running loop.

chapters.title: Deterministic Tests for Timeouts
points: Goal: assert on the outcome (a TimeoutError was raised, cleanup ran), never on real elapsed seconds. Wall-clock assertions are flaky under CI load.
Primitives: async with asyncio.timeout(delay) (3.11+) and asyncio.wait_for(aw, timeout). Since 3.11, asyncio.TimeoutError is the builtin TimeoutError.
Force a timeout deterministically by awaiting something that never finishes: await asyncio.Event().wait() under asyncio.timeout(0.01), then pytest.raises(TimeoutError).
asyncio.timeout(0), or a deadline already in the past, cancels at the next await, which gives an instant timeout with no sleeping.
Use Events or Futures that the test controls to decide when a dependency finishes, instead of sleep(0.5) and hoping the order works out.
Patch asyncio.sleep (for example with AsyncMock) so retry and backoff loops run instantly, then assert on the delays passed to it via await_args_list.
Virtual time: inject a clock, or use a fake-time plugin such as looptime that fast-forwards loop.time(). A 60 s timeout then runs in milliseconds.
Also check cancellation handling: after a timeout the inner task should be cancelled and its finally or cleanup should have run. Assert on that side effect.
Use asyncio.sleep(0) to yield exactly one scheduling step, letting pending callbacks run before an assertion.
Mistake: catching CancelledError and swallowing it inside the timed code. asyncio.timeout can then no longer convert it into TimeoutError, so the timeout silently fails.

chapters.title: Cheatsheet: Async Testing & Debugging
points: Run async tests: @pytest.mark.asyncio (strict mode) or asyncio_mode = auto. Standard-library alternative: IsolatedAsyncioTestCase with asyncSetUp and addAsyncCleanup.
Share a loop: @pytest.mark.asyncio(loop_scope='module') and @pytest_asyncio.fixture(loop_scope='session'). Keep test and fixture loop scopes aligned.
Mock async code with AsyncMock(return_value=..., side_effect=...), then assert_awaited_once_with(...). Use MagicMock for 'async with' and 'async for'.
Debug mode: asyncio.run(debug=True), PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1 or -X dev, plus logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG).
Blocking calls: tune loop.slow_callback_duration and move work to asyncio.to_thread().
Missing awaits: -X tracemalloc=25 plus -W error::RuntimeWarning.
Hangs: loop over asyncio.all_tasks() and call t.print_stack(). Name tasks with create_task(name=...). On 3.14, use python -m asyncio pstree PID.
Timeouts: under asyncio.timeout(0.01), await an Event that is never set; patch sleep; use virtual time; assert outcomes, not durations.

Warning decoder: 'never awaited' means a missing await; 'destroyed but pending' means a lost reference; 'different loop' means a loop_scope mismatch; 'exception never retrieved' means an unobserved task.
